Spectral and Additive Combinatorial Methods for Cycles and Absorbing Sets in Lifted-Product Quantum LDPC Codes

Aida Abiad ††thanks: a.abiad.monge@tue.nl, Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Eindhoven University of Technology, The Netherlands; Department of Mathematics and Data Science of Vrije Universiteit Brussel, Belgium    Nichola Castriota ††thanks: Nichola.Castriota@UGent.be, Department of Mathematics: Analysis, Logic and Discrete Mathematics, Ghent University, Belgium
Abstract

The finite-length performance of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes under iterative decoding is governed by small substructures of the Tanner graph, principally short cycles and absorbing sets. While the classical theory of these substructures for quasi-cyclic codes is well developed through discrete Fourier transform (DFT) methods, these tools do not directly address the two-block tensor structure HX=[H~1∣I⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\,\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}\,] of the lifted-product (quasi-cyclic generalised hypergraph product, QC-GHP) codes that dominate current quantum LDPC constructions.

In this paper we develop a quantum-specific spectral framework that exploits this structure. At its core is a DFT block-diagonalisation of HX​HXTH_{X}H_{X}^{T} that reduces moment-trace and cycle computations from an (r1​ℓ)×(r1​ℓ)(r_{1}\ell)\times(r_{1}\ell) matrix to a sum of ℓ\ell small r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1} Hermitian matrices, with the second block entering only as a scalar shift. From this result we derive a closed-form 44-cycle count for generalised bicycle codes via additive energies, a joint Sidon characterisation of girth 66 in the spirit of Fossorier’s classical criterion, a Fourier expression for the number of (3,3)(3,3) elementary absorbing sets in column-weight-33 codes via the Wang–Dolecek–Wesel triangle bijection, and a lower bound on stopping-set sizes using the expander mixing lemma.

Keywords: quantum LDPC codes, CSS codes, lifted product codes, generalised bicycle codes, Tanner graph, absorbing sets, stopping sets, discrete Fourier transform, additive energy, Sidon sets, expander mixing lemma

1 Introduction

Error-correcting codes underlie every modern communication and storage system, from cellular networks to deep-space links to the read channels in solid-state drives. In the quantum setting they play an even more fundamental role: physical qubits lose their state on microsecond timescales, so any scalable architecture must encode its information into a quantum error-correcting code able to detect and repair faults faster than they accumulate. Low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, introduced by Gallager [20] for the classical setting and later studied in the quantum setting, beginning with the sparse-graph constructions of MacKay, Mitchison, and McFadden [32] and notably through the generalised-bicycle construction of Kovalev and Pryadko [29], are among the leading candidate families for both regimes because they admit fast iterative decoders whose complexity grows only linearly with the block length.

In practice, at the realistic block lengths used in hardware, the iterative decoder of an LDPC code does not meet the asymptotic guarantees promised by coding theory: its failure probability eventually flattens out as the noise decreases, and the configurations responsible for this error floor are small recurring patterns in the bipartite Tanner graph associated to the code’s parity-check matrix [41, 16]. Two such patterns have repeatedly been singled out. Short cycles disrupt the independence assumptions on which iterative decoding rests and cause the decoder to oscillate, and absorbing sets are small vertex configurations where erroneous messages reinforce one another and become locally stable; the latter have been recognised as the dominant failure mechanism of iterative decoders across a wide range of channels [16, 33]. Morris, Pllaha, and Kelley [34] have recently shown that absorbing sets also drive decoder failure in Calderbank–Shor–Steane (CSS) quantum LDPC codes, so the same two graphical patterns govern the finite-length performance of classical and quantum LDPC codes alike.

Controlling these patterns turns the engineering question of code design into a combinatorial problem: how many few short cycles can a sparse Tanner graph have, and how small can its absorbing sets be? On the classical side, a considerable amount of work tackles this question through the spectrum of the parity-check matrix. For quasi-cyclic (QC) LDPC codes built from a cyclic lift, the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) block-diagonalises the relevant matrices and reduces cycle counts to small eigenvalue computations: this is the eigenvalue reduction of Smarandache and Flanagan [43] and the directed-edge-matrix recipe of Karimi and Banihashemi [27], while Fossorier [19] characterised the girth of QC codes built from circulant permutation matrices through exponent-difference conditions and Wang, Dolecek, and Wesel [48] gave a bijection between the smallest absorbing sets of column-weight-33 codes and triangles in an associated graph. On the quantum side, by contrast, cycle and absorbing-set counts of concrete code families have so far been obtained largely by direct enumeration [38] rather than through structural spectral tools, and the absorbing-set theory of CSS codes is only beginning to be developed [34]. A main obstacle is that the leading quantum LDPC constructions, the lifted-product (and quasi-cyclic generalised hypergraph product, QC-GHP) codes of Panteleev and Kalachev [38], have an XX-check matrix of the two-block tensor form HX=[H~1∣I⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\,\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}\,], which the single-block classical DFT machinery does not directly address.

In this work we address this gap by developing a quantum-specific spectral framework that exploits the two-block tensor form rather than working around it (Theorem 4.1). The main tool is a DFT block-diagonalisation of HX​HXTH_{X}H_{X}^{T} that captures the contribution of the second block as a scalar shift, reducing moment-trace and cycle computations on an (r1​ℓ)×(r1​ℓ)(r_{1}\ell)\times(r_{1}\ell) ambient matrix to a sum of ℓ\ell small r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1} Hermitian matrices. As a consequence of the proposed spectral framework, we obtain, for generalised bicycle (GB) codes, a closed-form count of 44-cycles in terms of the additive energies of the support sets of the defining polynomials (Proposition 4.9) together with a joint Sidon-type characterisation of girth 66 (Corollary 4.11) that parallels, in the single-circulant setting, Fossorier’s classical exponent-difference criterion [19]; through the triangle bijection of Wang, Dolecek, and Wesel [48], we derive a Fourier expression for the number of (3,3)(3,3) elementary absorbing sets in column-weight-33 QC-GHP codes (Proposition 4.17), addressing an enumeration question raised by the absorbing-set framework of Morris, Pllaha, and Kelley [34]; and, applying the bipartite expander mixing lemma through the second-largest singular value of HXH_{X} obtained from the same Fourier matrices, we show a spectral lower bound on the stopping distance of a QC-GHP code (Proposition 5.1). All of these expressions are computable in closed form from the polynomial data of the lifted-product construction, and together they specialise and unify the classical single-block spectral methods of [43, 27, 19, 48] to the quantum two-block setting.

2 Preliminaries

This section the needed graph-theoretic, coding-theoretic, quantum, and spectral background used throughout the paper.

2.1 Graph theory background

All graphs are finite and simple. For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with vertex set VV and edge set EE, we write N⁡(v)={u:{u,v}∈E}N(v)=\{u:\{u,v\}\in E\} for the neighbourhood of a vertex, deg⁡(v)=dv=|N⁡(v)|\deg(v)=d_{v}=|N(v)| for its degree, and N⁡(S)=⋃v∈SN⁡(v)N(S)=\bigcup_{v\in S}N(v). For S⊆VS\subseteq V, the induced subgraph on SS is G⁡[S]=GSG[S]=G_{S}; when DD is the vertex set of a substructure such as an absorbing set (Definition 2.8) we abbreviate 𝒢⁡[D]\mathcal{G}[D] by 𝒢D\mathcal{G}_{D}. The girthg⁡(G)g(G) is the length of a shortest cycle (with g⁡(G)=∞g(G)=\infty if GG is acyclic). A graph is dd-regular if every vertex has degree dd; a bipartite graph G=(VL,VR,E)G=(V_{L},V_{R},E), in which every edge joins VLV_{L} to VRV_{R}, is (dL,dR)(d_{L},d_{R})-biregular if all left vertices have degree dLd_{L} and all right vertices degree dRd_{R}. A bipartite graph has no odd cycle, so its girth, if finite, is an even integer at least 44. We refer to [6] for standard graph-theoretic background.

Definition 2.1 (Adjacency and biadjacency matrices).

Let GG be a graph with vertex set V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\}. The adjacency matrix of GG is the n×nn\times n symmetric 00-11 matrix AGA_{G} defined by (AG)i​j=1(A_{G})_{ij}=1 iff {vi,vj}∈E\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\in E. For a bipartite graph G=(VL,VR,E)G=(V_{L},V_{R},E) with |VL|=m|V_{L}|=m, |VR|=n|V_{R}|=n, the biadjacency matrix H∈{0,1}m×nH\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n} has Hi​j=1H_{ij}=1 iff the ii-th left vertex is adjacent to the jj-th right vertex. The full adjacency matrix is then the block matrix

AG=(0HHT0).A_{G}\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}0&H\\ H^{T}&0\end{pmatrix}.
Theorem 2.1 (Walk counts via matrix powers, [6]).

For any graph GG with adjacency matrix AGA_{G} and any integer k≥0k\geq 0, the entry (AGk)u​v(A_{G}^{k})_{uv} counts walks of length kk from vertex uu to vertex vv in GG. Consequently,

tr⁡(AGk)=#⁡{closed walks of length k in G}.\operatorname{tr}(A_{G}^{k})\;=\;\#\{\text{closed walks of length $k$ in $G$}\}.

The bipartite specialisation of Theorem 2.1 through the biadjacency matrix is stated as Lemma 2.2.

2.2 Coding theory background

Let 𝔽2={0,1}\mathbb{F}_{2}=\{0,1\}. For x∈𝔽2nx\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, the support is supp⁡(x)={i:xi=1}\mathrm{supp}(x)=\{i:x_{i}=1\} and the Hamming weight is wt⁡(x)=|supp⁡(x)|\mathrm{wt}(x)=|\mathrm{supp}(x)|. A (binary) linear code 𝒞⊆𝔽2n\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} of dimension kk (parameters [n,k][n,k], rate k/nk/n) is the kernel {x∈𝔽2n:H​x=0}\{x\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}:Hx=0\} of a parity-check matrix H∈𝔽2m×nH\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times n} (with m≥n−km\geq n-k); its minimum distance d=min{wt(x):x∈𝒞,x≠0}d=\min\{\mathrm{wt}(x):x\in\mathcal{C},\,x\neq 0\} equals the smallest size of a nonzero codeword support, and we write the parameters as [n,k,d][n,k,d]. The definition extends verbatim over any finite field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}; all codes here are binary (in the quantum case via the symplectic representation of Pauli operators, see §2.3.1).

Definition 2.2 (LDPC code).

A low-density parity-check (LDPC) code is a linear code that admits a sparse parity-check matrix HH, meaning each row and each column of HH has a small (constant or slowly-growing) number of nonzero entries relative to the block length nn.

A parity-check matrix has column weight γ\gamma (resp. row weight kk) if every column (resp. row) contains exactly γ\gamma (resp. kk) ones; the code is then (γ,k)(\gamma,k)-regular. Sparsity is asymptotic and has no sharp threshold at finite block length.

Definition 2.3 (Tanner graph, [46]).

Given a parity check matrix HH of a linear code 𝒞\mathcal{C}, its bipartite Tanner graph representation is the graph 𝒢=(V,W,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,W;E) where the vertex sets VV and WW correspond to the codeword coordinates and the parity check equations, and are called variable and check nodes, respectively. EE is the set of edges. For vi∈Vv_{i}\in V and cj∈Wc_{j}\in W, the edge (vi,cj)∈E(v_{i},c_{j})\in E if and only if hj,i=1h_{j,i}=1 in HH.

A code does not have a unique Tanner graph, as 𝒢\mathcal{G} depends on the choice of parity-check matrix. Being bipartite, 𝒢\mathcal{G} has even girth (≥4\geq 4) whenever finite. A code’s parameters are reflected in 𝒢\mathcal{G}: n=|V|n=|V|, m=|W|≥n−km=|W|\geq n-k (with equality when the rows of HH are independent), and dd equals the smallest size of a nonempty set S⊆VS\subseteq V such that every check in N⁡(S)N(S) has even degree in 𝒢⁡[S∪N⁡(S)]\mathcal{G}[S\cup N(S)].

2.2.1 Critical substructures: stopping, trapping, and absorbing sets

Throughout this subsection, 𝒢=(V,W,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,W;E) is the Tanner graph of a binary linear code 𝒞\mathcal{C} with parity-check matrix HH, and degrees are taken in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. All definitions are purely graph-theoretic and extend verbatim to non-binary linear codes.

Definition 2.4 (Stopping set, [12]).

A stopping set SS in a Tanner graph 𝒢=(V,W,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,W;E) is a subset S⊆VS\subseteq V of variable nodes such that every check node in the neighborhood N⁡(S)N(S) is connected to SS by at least two edges. Equivalently, the subgraph induced by S∪N⁡(S)S\cup N(S) contains no check node of degree one.

On the binary erasure channel, iterative decoding fails to recover the codeword iff the set of erased positions contains a stopping set [12, 42]; the stopping distance is the size of the smallest non-empty stopping set. See Figure 1(a).

Definition 2.5 ((a,b)(a,b)-trapping set, [41]).

An (a,b)(a,b)-trapping set TT in a Tanner graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a subset of aa variable nodes whose induced subgraph 𝒢T\mathcal{G}_{T} contains exactly bb odd-degree check nodes.

Figure 1(b) shows a (2,2)(2,2)-trapping set T={v1,v2}T=\{v_{1},v_{2}\} with its two odd-degree checks drawn in red.

Definition 2.6 (Elementary, leafless, and non-elementary trapping sets, [11]).

A trapping set is called elementary (ETS) if every check node in its induced subgraph has degree one or two. An elementary trapping set is leafless (LETS) if, additionally, every variable node is adjacent to at least two degree-two (satisfied) check nodes. An ETS that is not leafless is called an ETS with leaf (ETSL). A trapping set that is not elementary is called a non-elementary trapping set (NETS).

A related global construction is the variable-node graph, attached to the Tanner graph itself rather than to one of its substructures.

Definition 2.7 (Variable-node graph).

The variable-node graph of a Tanner graph 𝒢=(V,W,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,W;E), denoted GV​NG^{VN}, is the simple graph on the variable set VV in which u,v∈Vu,v\in V are adjacent iff there exists a check c∈Wc\in W with {u,c},{v,c}∈E\{u,c\},\{v,c\}\in E. When g⁡(𝒢)≥6g(\mathcal{G})\geq 6, any such pair {u,v}\{u,v\} shares at most one common check, so GV​NG^{VN} has no multi-edges.

Absorbing sets refine trapping sets by adding a local stability condition: every variable node in the set has strictly more satisfied (even-degree) than unsatisfied (odd-degree) check neighbours in the induced subgraph [14, 15]. This local majority is what makes absorbing sets “absorb” the decoder [16].

Definition 2.8 ((a,b)(a,b)-absorbing set, [14, 15]).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a Tanner graph and 𝒜⊆V\mathcal{A}\subseteq V a subset of aa variable nodes. For each variable v∈𝒜v\in\mathcal{A}, write eve_{v} (resp. ovo_{v}) for the number of check neighbours of vv in 𝒢𝒜\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{A}} whose degree in 𝒢𝒜\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{A}} is even (resp. odd). The set 𝒜\mathcal{A} is an (a,b)(a,b)-absorbing set if exactly bb check nodes in 𝒢𝒜\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{A}} have odd degree and ev>ove_{v}>o_{v} for every v∈𝒜v\in\mathcal{A}. An absorbing set is elementary if every check node in 𝒢𝒜\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{A}} has degree 11 or 22 (equivalently, the underlying (a,b)(a,b)-trapping set is an ETS in the sense of Definition 2.6).

2.3 Quantum LDPC codes

Quantum error-correcting codes encode kk logical qubits into nn physical qubits, embedding the logical state into a structured subspace of (ℂ2)⊗n(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes n}; see Breuckmann and Eberhardt [5] for a survey. We work with the stabilizer codes of Gottesman [21] and Calderbank-Rains-Shor-Sloane [7], and specifically with the Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) subclass, whose stabilizer factors into pure-XX and pure-ZZ generators. In the nn-qubit Pauli group any two elements commute or anticommute, and commutation is governed by the symplectic inner product on 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} [7, 21]; this is the structural reason CSS codes admit a binary-matrix description. We focus on the QLDPC subclass (Definition 2.10), whose running example is the quasi-cyclic generalized hypergraph product (QC-GHP) family of [38].

2.3.1 CSS codes

A stabilizer code is the joint +1+1 eigenspace of an abelian subgroup 𝒮⊆𝒫n\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{n} of the Pauli group [21, 7]; we work directly with the matrix description of the stabilizer.

Definition 2.9 (CSS code, [7, 21]).

A Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code is a stabilizer code whose stabilizer admits a set of generators that are either pure-XX (tensor products of II and XX only) or pure-ZZ. When the pure-XX generators are specified by a matrix HX∈𝔽2mX×nH_{X}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m_{X}\times n} (each row encodes the support of one generator) and the pure-ZZ generators by a matrix HZ∈𝔽2mZ×nH_{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m_{Z}\times n}, the commutation requirement on the stabilizer translates to the orthogonality condition

HX​HZT= 0(over ​𝔽2​).H_{X}H_{Z}^{\mkern 1.0muT}\;=\;0\qquad\text{(over }\mathbb{F}_{2}\text{).} (1)

The number of logical qubits encoded by the CSS code is

k=n−rank𝔽2​(HX)−rank𝔽2​(HZ),k\;=\;n-\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(H_{X})-\mathrm{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(H_{Z}),

and the minimum distance dd is the smallest weight of a Pauli operator that commutes with every stabilizer generator but does not lie in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The code is then said to have parameters [[n,k,d]][\![n,k,d]\!], where the double brackets distinguish quantum from classical parameters.

Equivalently, the row spaces of HXH_{X} and HZH_{Z} are mutually orthogonal, so the classical codes 𝒞X=ker⁡HX\mathcal{C}_{X}=\ker H_{X} and 𝒞Z=ker⁡HZ\mathcal{C}_{Z}=\ker H_{Z} form a nested pair 𝒞X⟂⊆𝒞Z\mathcal{C}_{X}^{\perp}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{Z}, and the CSS construction recovers a quantum code from any such pair.

2.3.2 QLDPC codes

Definition 2.10 (QLDPC code).

A quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) code is a CSS code in which both parity-check matrices HXH_{X} and HZH_{Z} are sparse in the sense of Definition 2.2.

QLDPC codes [32, 29] have become a central object in fault-tolerant quantum computing, with asymptotically good constructions due to Panteleev-Kalachev [37] and Leverrier-Zémor [30]. As classically, sparsity is asymptotic; in structured families the column and row weights of HX,HZH_{X},H_{Z} are fixed constants. Each CSS code carries two Tanner graphs, 𝒢X\mathcal{G}_{X} from HXH_{X} and 𝒢Z\mathcal{G}_{Z} from HZH_{Z} (Definition 2.3); these are the principal objects on which the decoding analyses in this work take place.

2.3.3 Syndrome-based decoding

When a Pauli error E=XeX​ZeZE=X^{e_{X}}Z^{e_{Z}} corrupts the encoded state, measuring the XX-type generators yields the XX-syndrome HX​eZ∈𝔽2mXH_{X}e_{Z}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m_{X}} and measuring the ZZ-type generators yields the ZZ-syndrome HZ​eXH_{Z}e_{X}. Syndrome-based decoding produces low-weight estimates e^X,e^Z\hat{e}_{X},\hat{e}_{Z} consistent with the observed syndromes [39], run block-by-block with one iterative message-passing decoder per Tanner graph [39, 40]. Decoding succeeds when e^X−eX∈rowspace⁡(HX)\hat{e}_{X}-e_{X}\in\mathrm{rowspace}(H_{X}) (a degenerate error acting trivially on the codespace) and produces a logical error otherwise.

The graph-theoretic substructures responsible for these failures are the quantum analogues of the stopping, trapping and absorbing sets of §2.2.1, taken up in Section 3. The verbatim graph-theoretic definitions (Definitions 2.4, 2.5, 2.8) carry over unchanged, since 𝒢X\mathcal{G}_{X} and 𝒢Z\mathcal{G}_{Z} are themselves classical bipartite graphs; what differs is that the decoder input is a measured syndrome rather than a corrupted codeword, so the substructures are characterised through the syndrome-matching analysis of Morris-Pllaha-Kelley [34]. In particular the b=0b=0 case acquires a genuinely quantum interpretation as a symmetric-stabilizer configuration on which iterative decoding oscillates rather than diverges [40, 34].

2.4 Spectral and Fourier background

We provide the discrete Fourier and circulant-matrix tools that will be used in the proposed spectral cycle-counting framework. Throughout, ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 is a positive integer and ω=e2​π​i/ℓ\omega=e^{2\pi i/\ell} is a primitive ℓ\ell-th root of unity.

2.4.1 Discrete Fourier transform on ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}

The characters of ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} are χj​(k)=ωj​k\chi_{j}(k)=\omega^{jk}, and the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of f:ℤℓ→ℂf:\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}\to\mathbb{C} is f^​(j)=∑k=0ℓ−1f⁡(k)​ω−j​k\hat{f}(j)=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell-1}f(k)\,\omega^{-jk}, with inverse f⁡(k)=1ℓ​∑jf^​(j)​ωj​kf(k)=\tfrac{1}{\ell}\sum_{j}\hat{f}(j)\,\omega^{jk} [9, Ch. 1]. The Parseval (energy) identity [9, §3.2] reads

∑k=0ℓ−1|f⁡(k)|2=1ℓ​∑j=0ℓ−1|f^​(j)|2.\sum_{k=0}^{\ell-1}|f(k)|^{2}\;=\;\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}|\hat{f}(j)|^{2}. (2)

We apply (2) to the symbol polynomials of circulant generator matrices, converting a time-domain sum into a sum over frequency-domain eigenvalues.

2.4.2 Circulant matrices and block-diagonalization

A matrix C∈ℂℓ×ℓC\in\mathbb{C}^{\ell\times\ell} is circulant if Ci​j=c(i−j)modℓC_{ij}=c_{(i-j)\bmod\ell} for some symbol c∈ℂℓc\in\mathbb{C}^{\ell}; equivalently C=∑k=0ℓ−1ck​SkC=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell-1}c_{k}\,S^{k} where SS is the cyclic shift matrix [9, §2.1]. The Fourier matrix FF with entries Fj​k=ωj​k/ℓF_{jk}=\omega^{jk}/\sqrt{\ell} is unitary and simultaneously diagonalises every circulant [9, Thm. 3.2.1]:

F​C​F∗=diag⁡(c^​(0),c^​(1),…,c^​(ℓ−1)),F\,C\,F^{*}\;=\;\mathrm{diag}\bigl(\hat{c}(0),\hat{c}(1),\ldots,\hat{c}(\ell-1)\bigr), (3)

where c^​(j)=∑kck​ωj​k\hat{c}(j)=\sum_{k}c_{k}\omega^{jk}; the same conjugation blockwise-diagonalises any block matrix of ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell circulants (replace FF by F⊗IrF\otimes I_{r} for blocks of size rr). Quasi-cyclic Tanner graphs, including the QC-GHP family of Example 3.2, have circulant-block biadjacency matrices, and (3) reduces their global cycle-counting problems to a sum over ℓ\ell smaller matrices {Mj}j=0ℓ−1\{M_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\ell-1}, the Fourier matrices of the protograph: this is the structural basis of Theorem 4.1.

2.4.3 Cycle counts from spectral traces

Theorem 2.1 specialises to bipartite graphs through the biadjacency matrix: the powers of H​HTHH^{T} count closed walks that begin and end on the same side.

Lemma 2.2 (Side-restricted trace identity; bipartite specialisation of Theorem 2.1, [6]).

Let G=(VL,VR,E)G=(V_{L},V_{R},E) be a bipartite graph with biadjacency matrix H∈{0,1}|VL|×|VR|H\in\{0,1\}^{|V_{L}|\times|V_{R}|}. For every integer k≥1k\geq 1 and every u∈VLu\in V_{L}, the diagonal entry ((H​HT)k)u​u\bigl((HH^{T})^{k}\bigr)_{uu} equals the number of closed walks of length 2​k2k in GG that begin and end at uu. Summing over u∈VLu\in V_{L},

tr⁡((H​HT)k)=#⁡{closed walks of length 2​k in G starting in VL}.\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl((HH^{T})^{k}\bigr)\;=\;\#\{\text{closed walks of length $2k$ in $G$ starting in $V_{L}$}\}.

The analogous identity holds for (HT​H)k(H^{T}H)^{k} and walks starting in VRV_{R}; by the cyclic invariance of trace the two counts are equal.

Proof.

From Definition 2.1 we have

AG2=(H​HT00HT​H),A_{G}^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}HH^{T}&0\\ 0&H^{T}H\end{pmatrix},

so AG2​kA_{G}^{2k} is block-diagonal with blocks (H​HT)k(HH^{T})^{k} and (HT​H)k(H^{T}H)^{k}. Therefore ((H​HT)k)u​u=(AG2​k)u​u\bigl((HH^{T})^{k}\bigr)_{uu}=\bigl(A_{G}^{2k}\bigr)_{uu} for u∈VLu\in V_{L}, and Theorem 2.1 identifies the right-hand side as the number of closed walks of length 2​k2k at uu. The remaining claims follow by summation and from tr⁡((H​HT)k)=tr⁡((HT​H)k)\operatorname{tr}\bigl((HH^{T})^{k}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H^{T}H)^{k}\bigr). ∎

Closed-walk counts overcount cycles because they include back-tracking steps and tree-shaped excursions; subtracting these via Möbius-type corrections converts tr⁡((H​HT)k)\operatorname{tr}\bigl((HH^{T})^{k}\bigr) into a closed-form count of cycles of length 2​k2k. The precise 44-cycle formula for quasi-cyclic Tanner graphs, expressed as a sum ∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡((Mj​Mj∗)2)\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}\bigl((M_{j}M_{j}^{*})^{2}\bigr) over the Fourier matrices of (3), is derived in Theorem 4.1; classical cycle-counting precursors appear in [27, 43].

3 Lifted-product QLDPC codes and the absorbing-set framework

Quantum LDPC (QLDPC) codes are among the leading current candidates for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation [22, 37, 30]. As in the classical case, their finite-length performance is determined not by asymptotics but by a small number of stable graphical configurations in the Tanner graph that cause persistent decoder failure [41, 15], and these critical substructures are far less understood in the quantum setting [8, 45, 34, 2] than in the classical one [11, 33, 3, 35, 36]. A systematic spectral graph-theoretic approach to QLDPC Tanner graphs, parallel to the adjacency-spectrum cycle counts used extensively for classical LDPC codes [10, 27, 4], has not yet appeared: the CSS commutation constraint and the lifted-product block structure pose additional obstructions. This work takes a first step via a discrete Fourier transform (DFT)-based cycle-counting framework for lifted-product Tanner graphs.

3.1 QLDPC codes and the absorbing-set framework

Both structural threads to date concern syndrome-based iterative decoding (§2.3.3), the natural decoding model for stabilizer codes [39]. Raveendran and Vasić [40] identify symmetric stabilizers, a genuinely quantum failure mode in which decoder degeneracy lets belief propagation oscillate between equivalent error estimates rather than converge. Morris, Pllaha, and Kelley [34] show that absorbing sets (Definition 2.8) are the dominant failure mechanism for syndrome-based iterative decoders: any (a,b)(a,b)-absorbing set with b≥1b\geq 1 is failure-inducing (its syndrome estimate stays 𝟎\bm{0}, permanently mismatching the input syndrome at the bb odd-degree checks), while the b=0b=0 case subsumes the symmetric-stabilizer phenomenon and governs the degenerate-versus-logical-error dichotomy [34]. For CSS hypergraph-product codes [47] the absorbing sets are completely characterised by the base matrices H1H_{1}, H2H_{2} and their transposes, so small base-code absorbing sets propagate to low-weight failure-inducing sets [34].

Absorbing sets thus give a single combinatorial object subsuming the symmetric-stabilizer formalism of [40], which is why subsequent QLDPC structural analyses [45, 8, 34] have converged on them. Moreover, the classical Hoory-type cage and girth lower bounds on absorbing-set sizes [25, 33] do not transfer to the QLDPC two-block form HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}], because the CSS commutation constraint HX​HZT=0H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0 forces girth at most 66 in any fully connected quasi-cyclic construction with column weight at least 33 [1], foreclosing the high-girth regime in which Hoory-type counting gives strong bounds.

3.2 Lifted-product QLDPC codes

We review the lifted-product construction of Panteleev and Kalachev [38] that produces the running QC-GHP example and the two-block form HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}] above.

Definition 3.1.

[38] Consider H1∈𝔽2r1×n1H_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{1}\times n_{1}}, H2∈𝔽2r2×n2H_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{2}\times n_{2}}, and GG a finite abelian group of size LL. Each g∈Gg\in G is associated with an L×LL\times L permutation matrix PgP_{g} over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} using the regular representation, defined by (Pg)h,k=1(P_{g})_{h,k}=1 if h=g​kh=gk; then Pg​Pg′=Pg​g′P_{g}P_{g^{\prime}}=P_{gg^{\prime}} and Pg−1=PgTP_{g^{-1}}=P_{g}^{T}.

Given a labeling of the nonzero entries of H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} by elements of GG, we regard H1H_{1} and H2H_{2} as matrices over the group algebra R=𝔽2​[G]R=\mathbb{F}_{2}[G]. For a matrix MM over RR, write M~\widetilde{M} for its binary lift, obtained by replacing each entry ∑gag​g\sum_{g}a_{g}\,g with the L×LL\times L matrix ∑gag​Pg\sum_{g}a_{g}P_{g} (so H~1∈𝔽2(r1​L)×(n1​L)\tilde{H}_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{(r_{1}L)\times(n_{1}L)}), and M∗M^{*} for its conjugate transpose, (M∗)i​j=(Mj​i)∗(M^{*})_{ij}=(M_{ji})^{*} with (∑gag​g)∗=∑gag​g−1\bigl(\sum_{g}a_{g}\,g\bigr)^{*}=\sum_{g}a_{g}\,g^{-1}; on lifts, M∗~=M~T\widetilde{M^{*}}=\widetilde{M}^{\,T}. The lifted product quantum CSS code is defined by its parity check matrices

HX=[H1⊗In2~|Ir1⊗H2∗~]andHZ=[In1⊗H2~|H1∗⊗Ir2~],H_{X}=\bigl[\,\widetilde{H_{1}\otimes I_{n_{2}}}\;\;\big|\;\;\widetilde{I_{r_{1}}\otimes H_{2}^{*}}\,\bigr]\qquad\text{and}\qquad H_{Z}=\bigl[\,\widetilde{I_{n_{1}}\otimes H_{2}}\;\;\big|\;\;\widetilde{H_{1}^{*}\otimes I_{r_{2}}}\,\bigr],

where the Kronecker products are taken over RR; the commutation condition (1) holds because HX​HZTH_{X}H_{Z}^{T} is the lift of H1⊗H2∗+H1⊗H2∗=0H_{1}\otimes H_{2}^{*}+H_{1}\otimes H_{2}^{*}=0 over RR. (For nonabelian GG the second factor must instead act through the right regular representation, see [37]; we do not need that generality here.) In the case r2=n2=1r_{2}=n_{2}=1 with H2=(b)H_{2}=(b), used throughout this paper, this reduces to HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗H~2T]H_{X}=[\tilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\tilde{H}_{2}^{T}] and HZ=[In1⊗H~2∣H~1T]H_{Z}=[I_{n_{1}}\otimes\tilde{H}_{2}\mid\tilde{H}_{1}^{T}].

Example 3.1 (Generalized bicycle codes as lifted products).

Take r1=n1=r2=n2=1r_{1}=n_{1}=r_{2}=n_{2}=1, so H1=(1)H_{1}=(1) and H2=(1)H_{2}=(1) are 1×11\times 1 matrices over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}. Let G=ℤℓ=⟨x∣xℓ=1⟩G=\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}=\langle x\mid x^{\ell}=1\rangle be the cyclic group of order ℓ\ell. Label the single nonzero entry of H1H_{1} by the group-algebra element a⁡(x)∈𝔽2​[x]/(xℓ−1)a(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}[x]/(x^{\ell}-1), and the single nonzero entry of H2H_{2} by the reversed polynomial b⁡(x−1)b(x^{-1}), so that H2∗=(b⁡(x))H_{2}^{*}=(b(x)). Writing AA and BB for the ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell circulant matrices of a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x), the parity check matrices of the lifted product code become

HX=[A∣B],HZ=[B⊤∣A⊤].H_{X}=[A\mid B],\qquad H_{Z}=[B^{\top}\mid A^{\top}].

This is precisely the generalized bicycle (GB) ansatz of Kovalev and Pryadko [29]. For instance, taking ℓ=24\ell=24, a⁡(x)=1+x2+x8+x15a(x)=1+x^{2}+x^{8}+x^{15}, and b⁡(x)=1+x2+x12+x17b(x)=1+x^{2}+x^{12}+x^{17} yields the [[48,6,8]][\![48,6,8]\!] code (code A3 in [38]).

Example 3.2 (A quasi-cyclic GHP code as a lifted product).

Now take r1=n1=7r_{1}=n_{1}=7, r2=n2=1r_{2}=n_{2}=1, G=ℤ63G=\mathbb{Z}_{63}, H2=(1)H_{2}=(1) with label b⁡(x)=1+x+x6b(x)=1+x+x^{6}, and H1H_{1} a 7×77\times 7 matrix over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} whose nonzero entries are labeled by monomials xi∈ℤ63x^{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{63}:

H1=(x270000x5411x270000x54x541x2700000x541x2700000x541x2700000x541x2700000x541x27).H_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{27}&0&0&0&0&x^{54}&1\\ 1&x^{27}&0&0&0&0&x^{54}\\ x^{54}&1&x^{27}&0&0&0&0\\ 0&x^{54}&1&x^{27}&0&0&0\\ 0&0&x^{54}&1&x^{27}&0&0\\ 0&0&0&x^{54}&1&x^{27}&0\\ 0&0&0&0&x^{54}&1&x^{27}\end{pmatrix}.

Lifting replaces each monomial xix^{i} with the corresponding 63×6363\times 63 cyclic permutation matrix and each 00 with the zero matrix; the single entry b⁡(x)=1+x+x6b(x)=1+x+x^{6} of H2H_{2} lifts to the 63×6363\times 63 circulant H~2=B\tilde{H}_{2}=B. The result is a CSS code with

HX=[H~1∣I7⊗B⊤],HZ=[I7⊗B∣H~1⊤],H_{X}=[\tilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{7}\otimes B^{\top}],\qquad H_{Z}=[I_{7}\otimes B\mid\tilde{H}_{1}^{\top}],

which is the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] generalized hypergraph product code (code B1 in [38]) with 18≤d≤2418\leq d\leq 24. (In [38] code B1 is presented with the labels 11 and x54x^{54} interchanged and with HX=[H~1∣I7⊗B]H_{X}=[\tilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{7}\otimes B], HZ=[I7⊗B⊤∣H~1⊤]H_{Z}=[I_{7}\otimes B^{\top}\mid\tilde{H}_{1}^{\top}]; the substitution x↦x−1x\mapsto x^{-1} combined with monomial rescalings identifies that presentation with the one used here, so both define the same code.) Its Tanner graph is (3,6)(3,6)-regular and has girth 66; the protograph of H1H_{1} is depicted in Figure 2.

3.3 Tanner graph properties of quasi-cyclic GHP codes

Regularity.

The Tanner graph of HXH_{X} (and symmetrically of HZH_{Z}) for the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code is (3,6)(3,6)-regular. More generally, when H1H_{1} has constant column weight w1w_{1} and constant row weight w1′w_{1}^{\prime} and H2H_{2} is 1×11\times 1 with label b⁡(x)b(x) of Hamming weight w2w_{2}, each variable node of HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗H~2T]H_{X}=[\tilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\tilde{H}_{2}^{T}] has degree w1w_{1} or w2w_{2} according to its column block, while each check node has degree w1′+w2w_{1}^{\prime}+w_{2}; in Example 3.2, w1=w2=3w_{1}=w_{2}=3 and w1′+w2=6w_{1}^{\prime}+w_{2}=6, recovering the (3,6)(3,6)-biregular graph. The biregular pair (γ,k)(\gamma,k) is exploited spectrally throughout: the DFT block-diagonalisation HX​HXT≅⨁jMjH_{X}H_{X}^{T}\cong\bigoplus_{j}M_{j} of Section 4 is a biregular-specific simplification, and the closed-form biregular cycle counts of Smarandache and Mitchell [44] lift to the QC-GHP setting (Remark 4.19).

Protograph and girth.

Lifting over G=ℤℓG=\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} preserves vertex degree, so biregularity of the protograph implies biregularity of the Tanner graph with the same degree pair [13, 28]. A protograph closed walk with ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}-labels g1,…,g2​kg_{1},\dots,g_{2k} lifts to ℓ\ell Tanner-graph cycles if and only if the alternating sum g1−g2+⋯−g2​k≡0(modℓ)g_{1}-g_{2}+\cdots-g_{2k}\equiv 0\pmod{\ell}, and to none otherwise [27]; this obstruction is the source of the Sidon-type arithmetic conditions on a⁡(x),b⁡(x)a(x),b(x) in Section 4. The Tanner graph of the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code has girth 66 [38], which is optimal within the QC framework: any fully connected quasi-cyclic construction with column weight at least 33 yielding a CSS code (HX​HZT=0H_{X}H_{Z}^{T}=0) has girth at most 66 [1], so the classical strategy of raising girth to suppress short cycles is structurally unavailable; girth beyond 66 requires column weight 22 [1].

Distance, trapping, and absorbing sets.

Panteleev and Kalachev report 18≤d≤2418\leq d\leq 24 for the [[882,24]][\![882,24]\!] code [38]; computing quantum minimum distance is hard in general [26], and sharp bounds are known only for generalized bicycle codes [49]. Raveendran and Vasić [40] show that symmetric-stabilizer trapping sets occur already in generalized bicycle codes (the r1=n1=1r_{1}=n_{1}=1 case) and that a layered decoding schedule mitigates them. For hypergraph-product codes the absorbing sets are governed by the base matrices H1H_{1}, H2H_{2} and their transposes [34]; how the group lift interacts with this structure for QC-GHP codes with circulant base matrices is identified as open in [34]. The chain-complex constructions of [34] exploit the symmetric tensor form HX,HGP=[H1⊗I∣I⊗H2T]H_{X,\mathrm{HGP}}=[H_{1}\otimes I\mid I\otimes H_{2}^{T}] and do not transfer directly to the asymmetric lifted-product form HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}]; the Sidon-type characterisation of Corollary 4.11 and the spectral 66-cycle count of Remark 4.13 give algebraic handles on this interaction in the girth-66 regime.

3.4 Trapping sets, absorbing sets, and stopping sets in QLDPC codes

Existing QLDPC trapping/absorbing-set work [45, 8] develops algorithmic methods (learning-aided trapping-set identification, decoder modifications, post-decoding correction) but yields no closed-form lower bounds on absorbing-set sizes; transferring classical biregular bounds to the two-block setting HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}] would require an analogue of the Zhao-Xiong-Ye-Yan [51] assumption that no two 88-cycles share a variable node, which for QC-GHP codes becomes a joint condition on the supports of H~1\widetilde{H}_{1} and b⁡(x)b(x) strictly stronger than the girth-66 Sidon condition of Corollary 4.11. In the classical setting, stopping sets (Definition 2.4) characterise the failure of iterative decoding on the binary erasure channel [12, 42] and the stopping distance lower-bounds the minimum distance; the QLDPC analogue carries the additional X/Z block structure, giving two coupled notions: X-stopping sets S⊆VL​(GX)S\subseteq V_{L}(G_{X}) and Z-stopping sets S⊆VL​(GZ)S\subseteq V_{L}(G_{Z}), each governing iterative decoding of one block of syndromes.

4 A spectral framework for cycle counting for lifted-product Tanner graphs

In this section we adapt and extend the classical spectral cycle-counting framework of Smarandache and Flanagan [43] and Karimi and Banihashemi [27] to the Tanner graphs of lifted-product QLDPC codes [38]. For cyclic lifts over G=ℤℓG=\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}, the biadjacency matrix of the Tanner graph block-diagonalises under the discrete Fourier transform, reducing cycle-counting traces to a sum over ℓ\ell small matrices [43, Thm. 1, Cor. 2], [27, Theorem 2]; in our setting this enters through Theorem 4.1 below. For classical QC-LDPC codes the reduction is due to Smarandache and Flanagan [43], who showed that the eigenvalues of the r​L×r​LrL\times rL matrix HT​HH^{T}H for an LL-fold cyclic lift of a J×rJ\times r protograph reduce to those of LL matrices of size r×rr\times r obtained by Fourier evaluation; Karimi and Banihashemi [27] give an alternative recipe via the directed edge matrix; and Smarandache and Mitchell [44] derive explicit closed forms for N2​kN_{2k} in any biregular Tanner graph, valid for k≤7k\leq 7.

On the quantum side, Zhang [50] carries out a finite-length combinatorial cycle analysis of the lifted product construction of [38] (and its left-right generalisation), focusing on dominant 88-cycles and proving a girth upper bound showing that 88-cycles are unavoidable regardless of the group-algebra elements, unlike the classical QC-LDPC case. Our framework is complementary: where Zhang enumerates 88-cycle topologies case by case, we develop a Fourier-spectral identity (Theorem 4.1) that translates short-cycle counts into traces of small matrices, applies uniformly to all even cycle lengths 2​k2k up to the girth bound, and yields the additive-energy/Sidon-type characterisations of §4 absent from [50]. This section specialises the classical single-block framework to the quantum two-block structure HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}] (Theorem 4.1, where the second block contributes only a scalar shift |b⁡(ωj)|2​Ir1|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}I_{r_{1}} to each block-diagonal matrix; see Remark 4.2), gives an additive-combinatorial reading of the GB-code 44-cycle formula via additive energies (Lemma 4.6, Proposition 4.9), and a joint Sidon condition characterising girth-66 GB codes (Corollary 4.11).

4.1 DFT block-diagonalisation

Consider a lifted product code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} (Definition 3.1) with base matrices H1∈𝔽2​[ℤℓ]r1×n1H_{1}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}]^{r_{1}\times n_{1}} and H2∈𝔽2​[ℤℓ]r2×n2H_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}]^{r_{2}\times n_{2}}, whose entries lie in the group ring 𝔽2​[ℤℓ]≅𝔽2​[x]/(xℓ−1)\mathbb{F}_{2}[\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}]\cong\mathbb{F}_{2}[x]/(x^{\ell}-1). We specialise to the QC-GHP case r2=n2=1r_{2}=n_{2}=1, so H2H_{2} is the 1×11\times 1 matrix with entry b⁡(x)∈𝔽2​[x]/(xℓ−1)b(x)\in\mathbb{F}_{2}[x]/(x^{\ell}-1). This covers the generalised bicycle ansatz (Example 3.1) and the QC-GHP family (Example 3.2), including the running [[48,6,8]][\![48,6,8]\!] and [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] codes; in the higher-rank case r2,n2>1r_{2},n_{2}>1 the matrix (5) becomes the commuting Kronecker sum Mj=A⁡(ωj)​A​(ωj)∗⊗In2+Ir1⊗B​(ωj)∗​B​(ωj)M_{j}=A(\omega^{j})A(\omega^{j})^{*}\otimes I_{n_{2}}+I_{r_{1}}\otimes B(\omega^{j})^{*}B(\omega^{j}), where B⁡(ωj)B(\omega^{j}) is the r2×n2r_{2}\times n_{2} Fourier evaluation of H2H_{2}, so its eigenvalues are the pairwise sums of those of the two factors and the trace analysis of §4 carries over (see Remark 4.2). The XX-parity check matrix is then

HX=[H~1|Ir1⊗B~T],H_{X}=\bigl[\,\widetilde{H}_{1}\;\big|\;I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{\mkern 1.0muT}\,\bigr],

where H~1\widetilde{H}_{1} is the (r1​ℓ)×(n1​ℓ)(r_{1}\ell)\times(n_{1}\ell) matrix obtained by replacing each group-ring entry of H1H_{1} with the corresponding ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell circulant matrix (and each zero entry with 0ℓ×ℓ0_{\ell\times\ell}), and B~\widetilde{B} is the ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell circulant associated with b⁡(x)b(x).

Let ω=e2​π​i/ℓ\omega=e^{2\pi i/\ell}. Every ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell circulant CC with first column (c0,c1,…,cℓ−1)T(c_{0},c_{1},\ldots,c_{\ell-1})^{T} is diagonalised by the DFT matrix FℓF_{\ell}: Fℓ​C​Fℓ∗=diag⁡(c^0,…,c^ℓ−1)F_{\ell}\,C\,F_{\ell}^{*}=\operatorname{diag}(\hat{c}_{0},\ldots,\hat{c}_{\ell-1}), where c^j=c⁡(ωj)=∑s=0ℓ−1cs​ωj​s\hat{c}_{j}=c(\omega^{j})=\sum_{s=0}^{\ell-1}c_{s}\,\omega^{js}. Since HXH_{X} has block structure [H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T][\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}] with (r1​ℓ)(r_{1}\ell) rows and (n1+r1)​ℓ(n_{1}+r_{1})\ell columns, conjugate on the left by UL=Ir1⊗FℓU_{L}=I_{r_{1}}\otimes F_{\ell} and on the right by UR=diag⁡(In1⊗Fℓ∗,Ir1⊗Fℓ∗)U_{R}=\operatorname{diag}(I_{n_{1}}\otimes F_{\ell}^{*},\;I_{r_{1}}\otimes F_{\ell}^{*}). For the first block, UL​H~1​(In1⊗Fℓ∗)U_{L}\,\widetilde{H}_{1}\,(I_{n_{1}}\otimes F_{\ell}^{*}) diagonalises each circulant sub-block independently. For the second block, since b⁡(x)b(x) has real (binary) coefficients, B~T\widetilde{B}^{T} corresponds to b⁡(x−1)b(x^{-1}) and satisfies Fℓ​B~T​Fℓ∗=diag⁡(b⁡(ω0)¯,…,b⁡(ωℓ−1)¯)F_{\ell}\,\widetilde{B}^{T}\,F_{\ell}^{*}=\operatorname{diag}(\overline{b(\omega^{0})},\ldots,\overline{b(\omega^{\ell-1})}), since b⁡(ω−j)=b⁡(ωj)¯b(\omega^{-j})=\overline{b(\omega^{j})} for real coefficients. Grouping indices by frequency jj rather than block index pp then gives the block-diagonal decomposition

H^X=⨁j=0ℓ−1H^X(j),H^X(j)=[A⁡(ωj)|b⁡(ωj)¯​Ir1]∈ℂr1×(n1+r1),\widehat{H}_{X}=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\widehat{H}_{X}^{(j)},\qquad\widehat{H}_{X}^{(j)}=\bigl[\,A(\omega^{j})\;\big|\;\overline{b(\omega^{j})}\,I_{r_{1}}\,\bigr]\in\mathbb{C}^{r_{1}\times(n_{1}+r_{1})}, (4)

where A⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j}) is the r1×n1r_{1}\times n_{1} matrix obtained by evaluating each group-ring entry of H1H_{1} at ωj\omega^{j}; see Figure 3.

Theorem 4.1 (Spectral trace formula for lifted product codes).

Let HXH_{X} be the parity check matrix of a lifted product code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} as above. For each j=0,…,ℓ−1j=0,\ldots,\ell-1, define the r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1} positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix

Mj=A⁡(ωj)​A​(ωj)∗+|b⁡(ωj)|2​Ir1.M_{j}\;=\;A(\omega^{j})\,A(\omega^{j})^{*}\;+\;|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}\,I_{r_{1}}. (5)

Then, by Lemma 2.2, the number of closed walks of length 2​k2k in the Tanner graph of HXH_{X} starting from check nodes is

tr⁡((HX​HXT)k)=∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡(Mjk)=∑j=0ℓ−1∑i=1r1λi​(Mj)k,\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{k}\bigr)\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}(M_{j}^{k})\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\sum_{i=1}^{r_{1}}\lambda_{i}(M_{j})^{k}, (6)

where λ1​(Mj)≤⋯≤λr1​(Mj)\lambda_{1}(M_{j})\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{r_{1}}(M_{j}) are the eigenvalues of MjM_{j}. Positive semidefiniteness of MjM_{j} ensures that all eigenvalues are non-negative real, so the right-hand side of (6) is a sum of non-negative real-valued powers and the cycle-count interpretation is consistent with the left-hand side being a real count.

Proof.

Treat HXH_{X} as a real 00-11 matrix, so HXT=HX∗H_{X}^{T}=H_{X}^{*}. With UL,URU_{L},U_{R} as above, the conjugated matrix H^X=UL​HX​UR\widehat{H}_{X}=U_{L}\,H_{X}\,U_{R} has the block-diagonal form (4) after the frequency-first permutation PP. As UL,URU_{L},U_{R} are unitary and PP is a permutation matrix (hence unitary), these similarities preserve traces of matrix powers, so

tr⁡((HX​HXT)k)=tr⁡((UL​HX​HXT​UL∗)k)=tr⁡((H^X​H^X∗)k)=∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡((H^X(j)​(H^X(j))∗)k),\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{k}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((U_{L}\,H_{X}H_{X}^{T}\,U_{L}^{*})^{k}\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\widehat{H}_{X}\widehat{H}_{X}^{*})^{k}\bigr)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}\Bigl(\bigl(\widehat{H}_{X}^{(j)}(\widehat{H}_{X}^{(j)})^{*}\bigr)^{k}\Bigr),

the last equality using the block-diagonal structure (see the spectral background §2.4 for matrix powers as walk counts and the trace-of-powers and DFT identities). Finally,

H^X(j)​(H^X(j))∗\displaystyle\widehat{H}_{X}^{(j)}(\widehat{H}_{X}^{(j)})^{*} =[A⁡(ωj)|b⁡(ωj)¯​Ir1]​[A​(ωj)∗b⁡(ωj)​Ir1]\displaystyle=\bigl[\,A(\omega^{j})\;\big|\;\overline{b(\omega^{j})}\,I_{r_{1}}\,\bigr]\begin{bmatrix}A(\omega^{j})^{*}\\ b(\omega^{j})\,I_{r_{1}}\end{bmatrix}
=A⁡(ωj)​A​(ωj)∗+|b⁡(ωj)|2​Ir1\displaystyle=A(\omega^{j})A(\omega^{j})^{*}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}I_{r_{1}}
=Mj,\displaystyle=M_{j},

which completes the proof. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Theorem 4.1 reduces the computation of traces of (r1​ℓ)×(r1​ℓ)(r_{1}\ell)\times(r_{1}\ell) matrix powers to a sum of traces of r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1} matrix powers. For the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code, this is a reduction from 441×441441\times 441 matrices to 6363 copies of 7×77\times 7 matrices.

For a single classical J×rJ\times r protograph parity-check matrix lifted by a factor LL, the eigenvalue reduction HT​H→{H⁡(ωj)​H​(ωj)T}j=0L−1H^{T}H\to\{H(\omega^{j})H(\omega^{j})^{T}\}_{j=0}^{L-1} that underlies Theorem 4.1 is due to Smarandache and Flanagan [43], and the explicit cycle-count formulas N2​k=N2​k​({λi})N_{2k}=N_{2k}(\{\lambda_{i}\}) for k≤7k\leq 7 are derived in Smarandache and Mitchell [44] for any biregular Tanner graph. Karimi and Banihashemi [27] give a parallel DFT recipe via the directed edge matrix; the two approaches are equivalent up to a change of basis. What this section adds to that classical literature is the specialisation to the quantum two-block structure HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}]: the second block Ir1⊗B~TI_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T} contributes only a scalar shift |b⁡(ωj)|2​Ir1|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}I_{r_{1}} to each MjM_{j}, so the spectrum of MjM_{j} is that of A⁡(ωj)​A​(ωj)∗A(\omega^{j})A(\omega^{j})^{*} from the first block, shifted uniformly by the second. This scalar-shift form would not hold for a general two-block concatenation with independent column structure.

4.2 Applications

In this section we provide some applications of the proposed spectral framework. In particular we illustrate how to use the spectral trace formula of Theorem 4.1 in two directions: the scalar reduction for generalised bicycle codes, and the genuinely matrix-valued QC-GHP case worked out on the running [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code.

4.2.1 Specialisation to generalised bicycle codes

Corollary 4.3 (Scalar trace formula for GB codes).

When r1=n1=1r_{1}=n_{1}=1 (generalised bicycle codes), A⁡(ωj)=a⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j})=a(\omega^{j}) is a scalar, so MjM_{j} reduces to the scalar |a⁡(ωj)|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}, and the expression (6) becomes

tr⁡((HX​HXT)k)=∑j=0ℓ−1(|a⁡(ωj)|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2)k.\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{k}\bigr)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\bigl(|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}\bigr)^{k}. (7)
Proof.

Use Theorem 4.1 with r1=n1=1r_{1}=n_{1}=1, where A⁡(ωj)=a⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j})=a(\omega^{j}) is a scalar. ∎

4.2.2 Application to the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] QC-GHP code

This subsubsection applies the spectral trace formula (Theorem 4.1) to the genuinely matrix-valued QC-GHP case, computing the 44-cycle count of the running [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code. For QC-GHP codes A⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j}) is genuinely r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1}, so (5) no longer collapses to a scalar shift. We illustrate on the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code of Example 3.2, where a second layer of cyclic symmetry inside H1H_{1} yields the eigenvalues of each MjM_{j} in closed form.

Example 4.1 (Spectral cycle counting for the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code).

With ℓ=63\ell=63, r1=n1=7r_{1}=n_{1}=7, and b⁡(x)=1+x+x6b(x)=1+x+x^{6} as in Example 3.2, the protograph matrix

H1=x27​I7+S+x54​S2,H_{1}\;=\;x^{27}\,I_{7}\;+\;S\;+\;x^{54}\,S^{2},

is itself a polynomial in the 7×77\times 7 cyclic shift SS defined by (S)i,k=1(S)_{i,k}=1 iff k≡i−1(mod7)k\equiv i-1\pmod{7} (the three diagonals of H1H_{1} in Example 3.2 correspond to the three terms of this polynomial). Evaluating each group-ring entry at ωj\omega^{j}, where ω=e2​π​i/63\omega=e^{2\pi i/63}, gives the 7×77\times 7 matrix

A⁡(ωj)=ω27​j​I7+S+ω54​j​S2,A(\omega^{j})\;=\;\omega^{27j}\,I_{7}\;+\;S\;+\;\omega^{54j}\,S^{2},

which is itself a polynomial in SS, so it is simultaneously diagonalised with SS in the basis of ℤ7\mathbb{Z}_{7}-Fourier vectors. The eigenvalues of SS are η−m\eta^{-m} for m=0,…,6m=0,\ldots,6 with η=e2​π​i/7=ω9\eta=e^{2\pi i/7}=\omega^{9}, so the eigenvalues of A⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j}) are

μj,m=ω27​j+ω−9​m+ω54​j−18​m,m=0,…,6.\mu_{j,m}\;=\;\omega^{27j}\;+\;\omega^{-9m}\;+\;\omega^{54j-18m},\qquad m=0,\ldots,6. (8)

Since A⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j}) commutes with SS and is normal, A⁡(ωj)​A​(ωj)∗A(\omega^{j})A(\omega^{j})^{*} has eigenvalues |μj,m|2|\mu_{j,m}|^{2}, and so by Theorem 4.1 the matrix MjM_{j} has eigenvalues |μj,m|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2|\mu_{j,m}|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}. The spectral trace formula (6) therefore reduces to the explicit double sum

tr⁡((HX​HXT)k)=∑j=062∑m=06(|μj,m|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2)k,\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{k}\bigr)\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{62}\,\sum_{m=0}^{6}\,\bigl(|\mu_{j,m}|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}\bigr)^{k}, (9)

turning a 441×441441\times 441 trace computation into 441441 scalar evaluations of (8) followed by a kk-th power.

As a consistency check at k=1k=1: each A⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j}) has Frobenius norm squared ‖A⁡(ωj)‖F2=21\|A(\omega^{j})\|_{F}^{2}=21 (it has 2121 unimodular entries), so ∑m|μj,m|2=21\sum_{m}|\mu_{j,m}|^{2}=21 for every jj, giving ∑j,m|μj,m|2=63⋅21=1323\sum_{j,m}|\mu_{j,m}|^{2}=63\cdot 21=1323. By Parseval, ∑j|b⁡(ωj)|2=ℓ⋅wt⁡(b)=189\sum_{j}|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}=\ell\cdot\operatorname{wt}(b)=189, so ∑j,m|b⁡(ωj)|2=7⋅189=1323\sum_{j,m}|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}=7\cdot 189=1323. The two contributions sum to tr⁡(HX​HXT)=2646=6⋅441\operatorname{tr}(H_{X}H_{X}^{T})=2646=6\cdot 441, as expected from the (3,6)(3,6)-regularity of the Tanner graph.

At k=2k=2, Lemma 4.8 below with ∑idc,i2=441⋅36=15876\sum_{i}d_{c,i}^{2}=441\cdot 36=15876 and ∑vdv​(dv−1)=882⋅6=5292\sum_{v}d_{v}(d_{v}-1)=882\cdot 6=5292 gives

C4=14​(tr⁡((HX​HXT)2)− 21168).C_{4}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{4}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{2}\bigr)\;-\;21168\bigr).
Corollary 4.4 (44-cycle count of the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code).

The Tanner graph of the [[882,24,d]][\![882,24,d]\!] code has girth 66 [38], equivalently C4=0C_{4}=0, so the protograph parameters (27,54)(27,54) together with b⁡(x)=1+x+x6b(x)=1+x+x^{6} satisfy the closed-form identity

∑j=062∑m=06(|μj,m|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2)2= 21168.\sum_{j=0}^{62}\sum_{m=0}^{6}\bigl(|\mu_{j,m}|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}\bigr)^{2}\;=\;21168. (10)
Proof.

Substitute the exponents (27,54)(27,54), the modulus ℓ=63\ell=63, and b⁡(x)=1+x+x6b(x)=1+x+x^{6} into the double sum (9) at k=2k=2, whose value is tr⁡((HX​HXT)2)\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{2}\bigr). Since the girth is 66 we have C4=0C_{4}=0, so the k=2k=2 reduction C4=14​(tr⁡((HX​HXT)2)−21168)C_{4}=\tfrac{1}{4}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{2}\bigr)-21168\bigr) forces tr⁡((HX​HXT)2)=21168\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{2}\bigr)=21168, which is the left-hand side of (10). ∎

The identity (10) is a sharp 44-cycle test: any modification of the exponents (27,54)(27,54) or of b⁡(x)b(x) that violates it introduces 44-cycles into the Tanner graph, and every nonnegative deviation from 2116821168 equals 4​C44C_{4}.

4.3 Cycle counts via additive energy

Next we connect the formula (7) to additive combinatorics over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}, so that C4=0C_{4}=0 becomes an arithmetic condition on the supports Sa,Sb⊂ℤℓS_{a},S_{b}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} rather than a closed-walk count. Write Sa=supp⁡(a)⊂ℤℓS_{a}=\operatorname{supp}(a)\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} and Sb=supp⁡(b)S_{b}=\operatorname{supp}(b) for the supports of a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x).

Definition 4.1 (Additive energy and cross-energy).

The additive energy of a set S⊂ℤℓS\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} is

E⁡(S)=|{(i,k,p,q)∈S4:i+p≡k+q(modℓ)}|=∑d∈ℤℓrd​(S)2,E(S)=\bigl|\bigl\{(i,k,p,q)\in S^{4}:i+p\equiv k+q\pmod{\ell}\bigr\}\bigr|=\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}}r_{d}(S)^{2},

where rd​(S)=|{(x,y)∈S2:x−y≡d}|r_{d}(S)=|\{(x,y)\in S^{2}:x-y\equiv d\}|. The cross-energy of the sets SaS_{a} and Sb⊂ℤℓS_{b}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} is

E⁡(Sa,Sb)=∑d∈ℤℓrd​(Sa)⋅rd​(Sb).E(S_{a},S_{b})=\sum_{d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}}r_{d}(S_{a})\cdot r_{d}(S_{b}).
Example 4.2.

For S={0,1,3}⊂ℤ7S=\{0,1,3\}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{7}, the difference counts are r0​(S)=3r_{0}(S)=3 and r±1​(S)=r±2​(S)=r±3​(S)=1r_{\pm 1}(S)=r_{\pm 2}(S)=r_{\pm 3}(S)=1, giving E⁡(S)=9+6=15E(S)=9+6=15 (Figure 4). Proposition 4.9 below expresses the 44-cycle count of a generalised bicycle code through these quantities.

Remark 4.5.

Since r−d​(S)=rd​(S)r_{-d}(S)=r_{d}(S) for any S⊂ℤℓS\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} (by the substitution (x,y)↦(y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)), the definition E⁡(Sa,Sb)=∑drd​(Sa)​rd​(Sb)E(S_{a},S_{b})=\sum_{d}r_{d}(S_{a})\,r_{d}(S_{b}), which naturally counts quadruples with i−k≡p−qi-k\equiv p-q (i.e. i−k−p+q≡0i-k-p+q\equiv 0), also equals the count of quadruples with i−k+p−q≡0i-k+p-q\equiv 0. This is the form that arises from the Fourier expansion in Lemma 4.6(ii).

Lemma 4.6.

Let S⊂ℤℓS\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} and a⁡(x)=∑s∈Sxsa(x)=\sum_{s\in S}x^{s}. Then:

  1. (i)

    ∑j=0ℓ−1|a⁡(ωj)|4=ℓ⋅E⁡(S)\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}|a(\omega^{j})|^{4}=\ell\cdot E(S).

  2. (ii)

    For T⊂ℤℓT\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} with b⁡(x)=∑t∈Txtb(x)=\sum_{t\in T}x^{t}, ∑j=0ℓ−1|a⁡(ωj)|2​|b⁡(ωj)|2=ℓ⋅E⁡(S,T)\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}\,|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}=\ell\cdot E(S,T).

Proof.

For (i), write |a⁡(ωj)|2=∑i,k∈Sωj⁡(i−k)|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}=\sum_{i,k\in S}\omega^{j(i-k)}, so that

|a⁡(ωj)|4=(∑i,k∈Sωj⁡(i−k))​(∑p,q∈Sωj⁡(p−q))=∑i,k,p,q∈Sωj⁡(i−k+p−q).|a(\omega^{j})|^{4}=\Bigl(\sum_{i,k\in S}\omega^{j(i-k)}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{p,q\in S}\omega^{j(p-q)}\Bigr)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,k,p,q\in S\end{subarray}}\omega^{j(i-k+p-q)}.

Summing over jj and using the orthogonality relation ∑j=0ℓ−1ωj​m=ℓ​ 1m≡0\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\omega^{jm}=\ell\,\mathbf{1}_{m\equiv 0} gives

∑j=0ℓ−1|a⁡(ωj)|4=ℓ⋅|{(i,k,p,q)∈S4:i−k+p−q≡0}|=ℓ⋅E⁡(S).\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}|a(\omega^{j})|^{4}=\ell\cdot\bigl|\{(i,k,p,q)\in S^{4}:i-k+p-q\equiv 0\}\bigr|=\ell\cdot E(S).

For (ii), the same argument gives

∑j|a(ωj)|2|b(ωj)|2=ℓ⋅|{(i,k,p,q):i,k∈S,p,q∈T,i−k+p−q≡0}|,\sum_{j}|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}=\ell\cdot|\{(i,k,p,q):i,k\in S,\;p,q\in T,\;i-k+p-q\equiv 0\}|,

which equals ℓ⋅E⁡(S,T)\ell\cdot E(S,T) by Remark 4.5. ∎

Remark 4.7.

Lemma 4.6 gives two interchangeable ways to compute E⁡(S)E(S) in practice: combinatorially as ∑drd​(S)2\sum_{d}r_{d}(S)^{2} by enumerating differences (cost O⁡(|S|2+ℓ)O(|S|^{2}+\ell)), or analytically as 1ℓ​∑j|a⁡(ωj)|4\frac{1}{\ell}\sum_{j}|a(\omega^{j})|^{4} via an FFT (cost O⁡(ℓ​log⁡ℓ)O(\ell\log\ell)). The same alternative applies to E⁡(Sa,Sb)E(S_{a},S_{b}) via part (ii).

We also use the standard 44-cycle count in a bipartite graph via the trace of the squared adjacency matrix.

Lemma 4.8 (see e.g. [24]).

In a bipartite graph with biadjacency matrix HH (check nodes as rows, variable nodes as columns), the number of 4-cycles is

C4=14​(tr⁡((H​HT)2)−∑idc,i2−∑vdv​(dv−1)),C_{4}=\frac{1}{4}\Bigl(\operatorname{tr}\bigl((HH^{T})^{2}\bigr)-\sum_{i}d_{c,i}^{2}-\sum_{v}d_{v}(d_{v}-1)\Bigr),

where dc,id_{c,i} is the degree of check node ii and dvd_{v} is the degree of variable node vv.

Proof.

Write A=H​HTA=HH^{T}. The diagonal entry Ai​i=dc,iA_{ii}=d_{c,i} and the off-diagonal entry Ai​jA_{ij} for i≠ji\neq j counts the number of common variable-node neighbours of check nodes ii and jj; call this λi​j\lambda_{ij}. A 4-cycle is determined by a pair of check nodes {i,j}\{i,j\} and a pair of their common variable neighbours, so C4=∑i<j(λi​j2)C_{4}=\sum_{i<j}\binom{\lambda_{ij}}{2}. Now tr⁡(A2)=∑i,jAi​j2=∑idc,i2+∑i≠jλi​j2\operatorname{tr}(A^{2})=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}^{2}=\sum_{i}d_{c,i}^{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}\lambda_{ij}^{2}, so ∑i≠jλi​j2=tr⁡(A2)−∑idc,i2\sum_{i\neq j}\lambda_{ij}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(A^{2})-\sum_{i}d_{c,i}^{2}. Similarly, ∑i≠jλi​j=∑i,jAi​j−∑iAi​i=∑vdv2−∑vdv=∑vdv​(dv−1)\sum_{i\neq j}\lambda_{ij}=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}-\sum_{i}A_{ii}=\sum_{v}d_{v}^{2}-\sum_{v}d_{v}=\sum_{v}d_{v}(d_{v}-1), where the identity ∑i,jAi​j=∑vdv2\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}=\sum_{v}d_{v}^{2} holds because each variable node vv contributes 11 to Ai​jA_{ij} for each of the (dv1)2=dv2\binom{d_{v}}{1}^{2}=d_{v}^{2} pairs (i,j)(i,j) of check nodes it is adjacent to. Therefore

C4=∑i<j12​(λi​j2−λi​j)=14​(tr⁡(A2)−∑idc,i2)−14​∑vdv​(dv−1),C_{4}=\sum_{i<j}\tfrac{1}{2}(\lambda_{ij}^{2}-\lambda_{ij})=\tfrac{1}{4}\bigl(\operatorname{tr}(A^{2})-\textstyle\sum_{i}d_{c,i}^{2}\bigr)-\tfrac{1}{4}\textstyle\sum_{v}d_{v}(d_{v}-1),

using ∑i<j=12∑i≠j\sum_{i<j}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}. ∎

Proposition 4.9 (4-cycle formula for GB codes).

Let HX=[A~∣B~]H_{X}=[\widetilde{A}\mid\widetilde{B}] be the parity check matrix of a generalised bicycle code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} with wt⁡(a)=wa\operatorname{wt}(a)=w_{a} and wt⁡(b)=wb\operatorname{wt}(b)=w_{b}. The Tanner graph of HXH_{X} has ℓ\ell check nodes, each of degree dc=wa+wbd_{c}=w_{a}+w_{b}, and 2​ℓ2\ell variable nodes: ℓ\ell of degree waw_{a} (from the A~\widetilde{A} block) and ℓ\ell of degree wbw_{b} (from the B~\widetilde{B} block). The number of 4-cycles is

C4=ℓ4​(E⁡(Sa)+2​E​(Sa,Sb)+E⁡(Sb))−ℓ⁡((wa+wb)2+wa​(wa−1)+wb​(wb−1))4.C_{4}=\frac{\ell}{4}\bigl(E(S_{a})+2\,E(S_{a},S_{b})+E(S_{b})\bigr)-\frac{\ell\bigl((w_{a}+w_{b})^{2}+w_{a}(w_{a}-1)+w_{b}(w_{b}-1)\bigr)}{4}. (11)
Proof.

We use (7) with k=2k=2:

tr⁡((HX​HXT)2)=∑j=0ℓ−1(|a⁡(ωj)|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2)2.\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{2}\bigr)=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\bigl(|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}\bigr)^{2}.

Expanding the square and applying Lemma 4.6:

tr⁡((HX​HXT)2)\displaystyle\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{2}\bigr) =∑j|a⁡(ωj)|4+2​∑j|a⁡(ωj)|2​|b⁡(ωj)|2+∑j|b⁡(ωj)|4\displaystyle=\sum_{j}|a(\omega^{j})|^{4}+2\sum_{j}|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}+\sum_{j}|b(\omega^{j})|^{4}
=ℓ​E​(Sa)+2​ℓ​E​(Sa,Sb)+ℓ​E​(Sb).\displaystyle=\ell\,E(S_{a})+2\ell\,E(S_{a},S_{b})+\ell\,E(S_{b}).

Substituting into Lemma 4.8 with m=ℓm=\ell, ∑idc,i2=ℓ​(wa+wb)2\sum_{i}d_{c,i}^{2}=\ell(w_{a}+w_{b})^{2}, and ∑vdv​(dv−1)=ℓ​wa​(wa−1)+ℓ​wb​(wb−1)\sum_{v}d_{v}(d_{v}-1)=\ell\,w_{a}(w_{a}-1)+\ell\,w_{b}(w_{b}-1) gives the desired result (11). ∎

Remark 4.10.

Proposition 4.9 shows that the girth of a GB code Tanner graph is at least 6 if and only if

E⁡(Sa)+2​E​(Sa,Sb)+E⁡(Sb)=(wa+wb)2+wa​(wa−1)+wb​(wb−1).E(S_{a})+2\,E(S_{a},S_{b})+E(S_{b})=(w_{a}+w_{b})^{2}+w_{a}(w_{a}-1)+w_{b}(w_{b}-1).

The right-hand side is the contribution from “trivial” 4-tuples (those where the two pairs of indices coincide). The following corollary reformulates this as a condition from additive combinatorics.

Corollary 4.11 (Joint Sidon condition for girth-6 GB codes).

A generalised bicycle code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} with polynomials a⁡(x),b⁡(x)a(x),b(x) has girth at least 66 if and only if

rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb)≤1for all ​d≢0(modℓ),r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b})\leq 1\quad\text{for all }d\not\equiv 0\pmod{\ell}, (12)

where rd​(S)=|{(x,y)∈S2:x−y≡d(modℓ)}|r_{d}(S)=|\{(x,y)\in S^{2}:x-y\equiv d\pmod{\ell}\}|. In other words, the difference multisets of SaS_{a} and SbS_{b}, restricted to nonzero differences, must be disjoint and repeat-free when combined.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.9, C4=0C_{4}=0 if and only if E⁡(Sa)+2​E​(Sa,Sb)+E⁡(Sb)=(wa+wb)2+wa​(wa−1)+wb​(wb−1)E(S_{a})+2\,E(S_{a},S_{b})+E(S_{b})=(w_{a}+w_{b})^{2}+w_{a}(w_{a}-1)+w_{b}(w_{b}-1). Since E⁡(Sa)+2​E​(Sa,Sb)+E⁡(Sb)=∑d(rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb))2E(S_{a})+2\,E(S_{a},S_{b})+E(S_{b})=\sum_{d}(r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b}))^{2}, the left-hand side decomposes as

(r0​(Sa)+r0​(Sb))2+∑d≠0(rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb))2=(wa+wb)2+∑d≠0(rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb))2,(r_{0}(S_{a})+r_{0}(S_{b}))^{2}+\sum_{d\neq 0}(r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b}))^{2}=(w_{a}+w_{b})^{2}+\sum_{d\neq 0}(r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b}))^{2},

using r0​(S)=|S|r_{0}(S)=|S|. The right-hand side equals (wa+wb)2+wa​(wa−1)+wb​(wb−1)(w_{a}+w_{b})^{2}+w_{a}(w_{a}-1)+w_{b}(w_{b}-1). Since ∑d≠0rd​(Sa)=wa2−wa=wa​(wa−1)\sum_{d\neq 0}r_{d}(S_{a})=w_{a}^{2}-w_{a}=w_{a}(w_{a}-1) and likewise for SbS_{b}, the condition C4=0C_{4}=0 reduces to

∑d≠0(rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb))2=∑d≠0(rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb)).\sum_{d\neq 0}(r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b}))^{2}=\sum_{d\neq 0}(r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b})).

For non-negative integers xx, x2≥xx^{2}\geq x with equality iff x∈{0,1}x\in\{0,1\}, so

∑d≠0((rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb))2−(rd​(Sa)+rd​(Sb)))=0\sum_{d\neq 0}\bigl((r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b}))^{2}-(r_{d}(S_{a})+r_{d}(S_{b}))\bigr)=0

with each summand non-negative forces every summand to vanish, giving (12). ∎

Remark 4.12.

When Sb=∅S_{b}=\emptyset (i.e. a single circulant block), condition (12) reduces to rd​(Sa)≤1r_{d}(S_{a})\leq 1 for all d≠0d\neq 0, which is the classical definition of a Sidon set (or B2B_{2} set) in ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}. For a Sidon set S⊂ℤℓS\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}, counting nonzero differences gives |S|​(|S|−1)≤ℓ−1|S|(|S|-1)\leq\ell-1, so |S|≤ℓ+O⁡(1)|S|\leq\sqrt{\ell}+O(1) (cf. the Erdős–Turán bound for Sidon sets of integers [17]). For the joint condition (12), the combined difference set {x−y:(x,y)∈Sa2∪Sb2,x≠y}\{x-y:(x,y)\in S_{a}^{2}\cup S_{b}^{2},\,x\neq y\} must have no repeated elements, so

wa​(wa−1)+wb​(wb−1)≤ℓ−1,w_{a}(w_{a}-1)+w_{b}(w_{b}-1)\leq\ell-1,

giving an upper bound on the total weight wa+wbw_{a}+w_{b} achievable at girth 6 for a given ℓ\ell.

Remark 4.13 (Towards 66-cycle counts via additive 33-energies).

The same DFT identity extends to closed walks of length 66: by Theorem 4.1 with k=3k=3,

tr⁡((HX​HXT)3)=∑j=0ℓ−1(|a⁡(ωj)|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2)3.\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{3}\bigr)\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\bigl(|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}\bigr)^{3}.

Expanding the cube and applying the same Parseval calculation as in Lemma 4.6 (using the Parseval identity (2) of the spectral background §2.4) expresses each term via the additive 33-energy

T3​(S)=|{(i1,k1,i2,k2,i3,k3)∈S6:(i1−k1)+(i2−k2)+(i3−k3)≡0(modℓ)}|,T_{3}(S)\;=\;\bigl|\bigl\{(i_{1},k_{1},i_{2},k_{2},i_{3},k_{3})\in S^{6}\;:\;(i_{1}-k_{1})+(i_{2}-k_{2})+(i_{3}-k_{3})\equiv 0\pmod{\ell}\bigr\}\bigr|,

together with mixed cross-versions for SaS_{a} and SbS_{b}, via the identity ∑j|a⁡(ωj)|6=ℓ​T3​(Sa)\sum_{j}|a(\omega^{j})|^{6}=\ell\,T_{3}(S_{a}) (and analogously for higher mixed terms). Note that T3​(S)≠∑drd​(S)3T_{3}(S)\neq\sum_{d}r_{d}(S)^{3} in general: writing rd​(S)r_{d}(S) for the number of representations d=i−kd=i-k with i,k∈Si,k\in S, one has T3(S)=∑d1+d2+d3≡(modℓ)rd1(S)rd2(S)rd3(S)T_{3}(S)=\sum_{d_{1}+d_{2}+d_{3}\equiv 0\!\pmod{\ell}}r_{d_{1}}(S)\,r_{d_{2}}(S)\,r_{d_{3}}(S), which counts all difference-triples summing to 00 modulo ℓ\ell, whereas ∑drd​(S)3\sum_{d}r_{d}(S)^{3} counts only those with d1=d2=d3d_{1}=d_{2}=d_{3}; neither sum is contained in the other. Translating tr⁡((HX​HXT)3)\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{3}\bigr) into a 66-cycle count requires subtracting closed length-66 walks that are not simple cycles; under girth ≥6\geq 6 (i.e. assuming the Sidon condition (12)) these reduce to backtracking walks whose count is fixed by the local degree statistics of the Tanner graph. The resulting girth-88 criterion is then a higher-order arithmetic condition on the supports, analogous to Corollary 4.11 but strictly stronger; we do not work out the full bookkeeping here.

4.4 Spectral interpretation of the Wang-Dolecek-Wesel reduction in the QC-GHP setting

The cycle-counting formulas of Section 4 connect to absorbing sets, the dominant graphical cause of decoder failure, through a classical bijection of Wang, Dolecek and Wesel [48]. Recast in graph-theoretic language and combined with Theorem 4.1, it yields a closed-form spectral expression for the number of (3,3)(3,3) elementary absorbing sets in a QC-GHP code, addressing in the column-weight-33 case an enumeration question raised by Morris, Pllaha and Kelley [34] for QLDPC codes with circulant base matrices.

Throughout, assume the Tanner graph GG has constant variable-node degree γ=3\gamma=3 and girth at least 66, which covers the QC-GHP family above when H1H_{1} has column weight three and wt⁡(b)=3\operatorname{wt}(b)=3. Recall the variable-node graph GV​NG^{VN} from Definition 2.7; under girth ≥6\geq 6 it is simple.

Lemma 4.14 (Wang-Dolecek-Wesel [48], in GV​NG^{VN} language).

For a Tanner graph GG with γ=3\gamma=3 and g⁡(G)≥6g(G)\geq 6, the assignment A↦AA\mapsto A is a bijection between

  1. (a)

    elementary (3,3)(3,3)-absorbing sets of GG, and

  2. (b)

    simple 66-cycles of GG, equivalently the triangles K3K_{3} in GV​NG^{VN} realised by three pairwise distinct checks.

A triangle of GV​NG^{VN} realised by a single check of degree ≥3\geq 3 is not absorbing: that check has odd degree in GAG_{A}, so each of its three variables would have three odd and no even checks, violating the strong-majority condition.

Proof.

The correspondence is established in [48] via the cycle-consistency-matrix formalism for separable circulant-based codes; we give a graph-theoretic restatement valid for any Tanner graph satisfying the hypotheses.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow) Let A={u1,u2,u3}A=\{u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\} be an elementary (3,3)(3,3)-absorbing set. The total incidence count from AA is ∑iγ=9\sum_{i}\gamma=9. By elementarity each check in N⁡(A)N(A) has degree 11 or 22 in GAG_{A}; the b=3b=3 degree-11 checks contribute 33 incidences, leaving 66 incidences from 33 degree-22 checks, so |N⁡(A)|=6|N(A)|=6. The strong-majority condition forces each uiu_{i} to have at least 22 even-degree-check neighbours in GAG_{A}, so (with γ=3\gamma=3) exactly 22 degree-22 and 11 degree-11 check neighbour. Thus the 33 degree-22 checks form a triangle on {u1,u2,u3}\{u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\} in GV​NG^{VN}, realised by three pairwise distinct checks.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow) Conversely, given a triangle {u1,u2,u3}\{u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\} in GV​NG^{VN} realised by three pairwise distinct checks c12,c13,c23c_{12},c_{13},c_{23} (equivalently, a simple 66-cycle of GG), each uiu_{i} has its three checks split as the two pair-checks ci​j,ci​kc_{ij},c_{ik} (j,k≠ij,k\neq i) and one extra check ci′′c^{\prime\prime}_{i}. The check ci′′c^{\prime\prime}_{i} cannot also be incident to uju_{j} for any j≠ij\neq i, else uiu_{i} and uju_{j} would share two distinct checks (ci​jc_{ij} and ci′′c^{\prime\prime}_{i}), giving a 44-cycle and contradicting g⁡(G)≥6g(G)\geq 6. Thus ci′′c^{\prime\prime}_{i} has degree exactly 11 in GAG_{A}. The same argument shows ci′′≠cj′′c^{\prime\prime}_{i}\neq c^{\prime\prime}_{j} for i≠ji\neq j. So |N⁡(A)|=6|N(A)|=6, with 33 degree-22 and 33 degree-11 checks; each uiu_{i} has 22 even-degree and 11 odd-degree check neighbour in GAG_{A}, satisfying strong majority. So AA is an elementary (3,3)(3,3)-absorbing set. ∎

The variable-node graph admits a clean spectral description.

Lemma 4.15.

Let GG be a Tanner graph with biadjacency matrix HH, constant variable-node degree γ\gamma, and g⁡(G)≥6g(G)\geq 6. Then

AV​N=HT​H−γ​I,A_{VN}\;=\;H^{T}H\;-\;\gamma\,I,

and consequently for every k≥0k\geq 0

tr⁡(AV​Nk)=∑l=0k(kl)​(−γ)k−l​tr⁡((HT​H)l).\operatorname{tr}(A_{VN}^{k})\;=\;\sum_{l=0}^{k}\binom{k}{l}\,(-\gamma)^{k-l}\,\operatorname{tr}\bigl((H^{T}H)^{l}\bigr). (13)
Proof.

The off-diagonal entry (HT​H)u,u′(H^{T}H)_{u,u^{\prime}} counts the common check-neighbours of u,u′u,u^{\prime}, which is 00 or 11 under g⁡(G)≥6g(G)\geq 6 (else a 44-cycle); the diagonal entry equals the variable-node degree γ\gamma. So HT​H=AV​N+γ​IH^{T}H=A_{VN}+\gamma I. Identity (13) follows by binomial expansion of AV​Nk=(HT​H−γ​I)kA_{VN}^{k}=(H^{T}H-\gamma I)^{k} and linearity of trace. ∎

For QC-GHP codes the right-hand side of (13) is fully spectral:

tr⁡((HXT​HX)l)=tr⁡((HX​HXT)l)=∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡(Mjl)\operatorname{tr}((H_{X}^{T}H_{X})^{l})=\operatorname{tr}((H_{X}H_{X}^{T})^{l})=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}(M_{j}^{l})

for l≥1l\geq 1 by Theorem 4.1, while

tr⁡((HXT​HX)0)=tr⁡(I(n1+r1)​ℓ)=(n1+r1)​ℓ.\operatorname{tr}((H_{X}^{T}H_{X})^{0})=\operatorname{tr}(I_{(n_{1}+r_{1})\ell})=(n_{1}+r_{1})\ell.

Triangles in GV​NG^{VN} recover the 66-cycle count of GG:

Lemma 4.16.

For GG as above, the triangles of GV​NG^{VN} are of two kinds: those realised by three distinct checks, which are in bijection with the simple 66-cycles of GG, and those realised by a single check of degree at least 33. Consequently

#​K3​(GV​N)=N6​(G)+∑c∈W(deg⁡(c)3),\#K_{3}(G^{VN})\;=\;N_{6}(G)\;+\;\sum_{c\in W}\binom{\deg(c)}{3},

or equivalently

N6​(G)=16​tr⁡(AV​N3)−∑c∈W(deg⁡(c)3).N_{6}(G)\;=\;\tfrac{1}{6}\operatorname{tr}(A_{VN}^{3})\;-\;\sum_{c\in W}\binom{\deg(c)}{3}.
Proof.

Each edge of a triangle {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\} in GV​NG^{VN} is realised by a check: u,vu,v share cu​vc_{uv}, and likewise cv​w,cu​wc_{vw},c_{uw}, each pair sharing exactly one check since g⁡(G)≥6g(G)\geq 6. If two of these coincide, say cu​v=cv​w=cc_{uv}=c_{vw}=c, then cc is adjacent to all of u,v,wu,v,w, so c=cu​wc=c_{uw} as well; hence the three checks are either pairwise distinct or all equal. If they are pairwise distinct, the closed walk u​cu​v​v​cv​w​w​cu​w​uu\,c_{uv}\,v\,c_{vw}\,w\,c_{uw}\,u is a simple 66-cycle (a repeated vertex would force a cycle shorter than 66); conversely every simple 66-cycle of the bipartite graph GG alternates variable/check and projects to such a triangle, so this is a bijection. If the three checks are all equal to one check cc, then deg⁡(c)≥3\deg(c)\geq 3 and {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\} is one of its (deg⁡(c)3)\binom{\deg(c)}{3} neighbour-triples; no such triangle is a 66-cycle, and none is counted for two different checks (two checks adjacent to the same three variables would create a 44-cycle, impossible at g⁡(G)≥6g(G)\geq 6), giving ∑c(deg⁡(c)3)\sum_{c}\binom{\deg(c)}{3} single-check triangles. Since AV​NA_{VN} is the adjacency matrix of the simple graph GV​NG^{VN}, 16​tr⁡(AV​N3)=#​K3​(GV​N)\tfrac{1}{6}\operatorname{tr}(A_{VN}^{3})=\#K_{3}(G^{VN}), and the two displayed identities follow. ∎

Combining Lemmas 4.14, 4.15 and 4.16 with Theorem 4.1 gives the main result of this subsection: in the QC-GHP setting, the count of (3,3)(3,3) elementary absorbing sets, equivalently the 66-cycle count N6N_{6}, admits an explicit closed-form Fourier expression.

Proposition 4.17 ((3,3)(3,3)-absorbing-set spectral count for QC-GHP codes).

Let GXG_{X} be the XX-Tanner graph of a QC-GHP code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell} with γ=3\gamma=3 and g⁡(GX)≥6g(G_{X})\geq 6. Then

#⁡(elementary ​(3,3)​-absorbing sets)=N6​(GX),\#\,(\text{elementary }(3,3)\text{-absorbing sets})\;=\;N_{6}(G_{X}),

and

N6​(GX)=16​[∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡(Mj3)− 3​γ​∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡(Mj2)+ 3​γ2​∑j=0ℓ−1tr⁡(Mj)−γ3​(n1+r1)​ℓ]−∑c∈W(deg⁡(c)3).N_{6}(G_{X})\;=\;\frac{1}{6}\!\left[\,\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}(M_{j}^{3})\;-\;3\gamma\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}(M_{j}^{2})\;+\;3\gamma^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}(M_{j})\;-\;\gamma^{3}\,(n_{1}+r_{1})\,\ell\,\right]\;-\;\sum_{c\in W}\binom{\deg(c)}{3}. (14)

The bracket in Proposition 4.17 equals tr⁡(AV​N3)\operatorname{tr}(A_{VN}^{3}), so the first term equals 16​tr⁡(AV​N3)=#​K3​(GXV​N)\tfrac{1}{6}\operatorname{tr}(A_{VN}^{3})=\#K_{3}(G_{X}^{VN}); the correction ∑c(deg⁡(c)3)\sum_{c}\binom{\deg(c)}{3} removes the triangles of GXV​NG_{X}^{VN} induced by a single check of degree ≥3\geq 3 (Lemma 4.16). For a (γ,k)(\gamma,k)-biregular QC-GHP code with m=r1​ℓm=r_{1}\ell checks of degree kk it equals r1​ℓ​(k3)r_{1}\ell\binom{k}{3}; for the [[882,24]][\![882,24]\!] code this is 441​(63)=8820441\binom{6}{3}=8820. For generalised bicycle codes (r1=n1=1r_{1}=n_{1}=1), each MjM_{j} collapses to the scalar |a⁡(ωj)|2+|b⁡(ωj)|2|a(\omega^{j})|^{2}+|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}, and (14) reduces to a polynomial in those scalars together with the constant ∑c(deg⁡(c)3)=ℓ​(wa+wb3)\sum_{c}\binom{\deg(c)}{3}=\ell\binom{w_{a}+w_{b}}{3}, computable in O⁡(ℓ​log⁡ℓ)O(\ell\log\ell) time via FFT.

The combinatorial half,

#⁡(elementary (3, 3)-absorbing sets)=N6​(GX),\#(\text{elementary (3, 3)-absorbing sets})=N_{6}(G_{X}),

is the Wang-Dolecek-Wesel observation [48] in GV​NG^{VN} language. The spectral half, the closed-form expression (14) for N6​(GX)N_{6}(G_{X}) in terms of the QC-GHP Fourier evaluations A⁡(ωj)A(\omega^{j}) and b⁡(ωj)b(\omega^{j}), is the contribution of Section 4; the directed-edge-matrix DFT method of Karimi and Banihashemi [27] gives an equivalent count for classical QC-LDPC codes, but the explicit two-block QC-GHP form via the r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1} matrices MjM_{j} does not appear there.

Remark 4.18 (Other absorbing-set sizes).

For column-weight-33 girth-66 codes the smallest elementary absorbing-set types are (3,3)(3,3) and (4,2)(4,2), see [48]. The GV​NG^{VN} dictionary handles (4,2)(4,2) in principle: an elementary (4,2)(4,2)-absorbing set corresponds to an induced “K4K_{4} minus an edge” on four variables in GV​NG^{VN}, with a degree-11 check attached to each of the two vertices of GV​NG^{VN}-degree 22 within the configuration. Counting induced “K4K_{4} minus an edge” subgraphs requires tr⁡(AV​N4)\operatorname{tr}(A_{VN}^{4}) together with subgraph-elimination corrections, themselves expressible via the spectral data but tied to the additive T3T_{3} machinery of Remark 4.13; we defer this computation to future work. The case (4,0)(4,0) corresponds to induced K4K_{4} in GV​NG^{VN} but is generally rare or absent in the regime relevant to QC-GHP codes (where girth at most 66 is forced by the CSS commutation constraint [1]), so we do not develop it further.

Remark 4.19 (Comparison with adjacent classical QC-LDPC machinery).

This remark compares the spectral-trace identity of Theorem 4.1 with two adjacent classical pieces of QC-LDPC machinery, both of which yield cycle counts in the QC-GHP setting via slightly different routes: the directed-edge-matrix framework of Karimi-Banihashemi [27], and the moment-recursion of Smarandache-Mitchell [44]. The two approaches give equivalent answers up to a change of basis, but differ in what they require as input and what their output looks like. The directed-edge-matrix framework of Karimi and Banihashemi [27] gives, for any graph of girth gg, the clean cycle count Nk=tr⁡(Aek)/(2​k)N_{k}=\operatorname{tr}(A_{e}^{k})/(2k) for k<2​gk<2g, where AeA_{e} is the Hashimoto 2​|E|×2​|E|2|E|\times 2|E| directed-edge matrix; no trace-correction terms (cf. Lemma 4.15) are needed. For a QC protograph code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}, the matrix Ae2A_{e}^{2} has block-circulant structure with blocks of size |Eb|×|Eb||E_{b}|\times|E_{b}| (|Eb||E_{b}| = number of edges of the base graph), and the same DFT block-diagonalisation as Theorem 4.1 reduces NkN_{k} to a sum of traces of ℓ\ell small matrices. The construction applies verbatim to the XX-Tanner graph GXG_{X} of any QC-GHP or generalised bicycle code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}, yielding closed-form expressions for N4,N6,…,N2​g−2N_{4},N_{6},\ldots,N_{2g-2} via Fourier evaluations of base-graph data, on a larger ambient matrix (2​|E|2|E| vs. r1​ℓr_{1}\ell) but without the lower-cycle correction terms that appear in our adjacency-based identity. We do not develop this route further.

Complementarily, the Smarandache-Mitchell recursion [44, Cor. 4] expresses N2​jN_{2j} for 2≤j≤72\leq j\leq 7 in any (γ,k)(\gamma,k)-biregular Tanner graph as a polynomial in the moments μj≔Tr⁡((H​HT)j)\mu_{j}\coloneqq\operatorname{Tr}((HH^{T})^{j}) and the lower cycle counts N4,N6,…,N2​j−2N_{4},N_{6},\ldots,N_{2j-2}, under a girth hypothesis that grows with jj: girth ≥4\geq 4 for N4,N6N_{4},N_{6}, girth ≥6\geq 6 for N8,N10N_{8},N_{10}, and girth ≥8\geq 8 for N12,N14N_{12},N_{14}. By Theorem 4.1, μj=∑j′=0ℓ−1tr⁡(Mj′j)\mu_{j}=\sum_{j^{\prime}=0}^{\ell-1}\operatorname{tr}(M_{j^{\prime}}^{j}) in the QC-GHP setting; combined with the recursion this gives a Fourier expression for N2​jN_{2j} in terms of the same Fourier matrices. In particular, the girth-66 hypothesis under which the rest of this section operates already suffices for N8N_{8} and N10N_{10}, so these cycle counts of the running [[882,24]][\![882,24]\!] QC-GHP code (girth 66) are computable in closed form from its Fourier matrices; we do not work out the expressions here. Translating N2​j​(GX)N_{2j}(G_{X}) into an absorbing-set count beyond the (3,3)(3,3) bijection of Proposition 4.17 would require an analogue of Lemma 4.14 for length-2​j2j cycles in GXG_{X} (equivalently, jj-cycles in GV​NG^{VN} on jj distinct variables under a suitable girth hypothesis); we do not pursue this here.

5 Spectral lower bound on the QC-GHP stopping distance

Combining the bipartite version of the expander Mixing Lemma (Haemers [23]; see also [6, §4.3, 4.8]) with the Fourier matrices of Theorem 4.1 yields a spectral lower bound on the QC-GHP stopping distance.

Proposition 5.1 (Spectral gap bound on stopping-set size in QC-GHP codes).

Let GXG_{X} be the XX-Tanner graph of a (γ,k)(\gamma,k)-biregular QC-GHP code over ℤℓ\mathbb{Z}_{\ell}, with m=r1​ℓm=r_{1}\ell check nodes and Fourier matrices {Mj}j=0ℓ−1\{M_{j}\}_{j=0}^{\ell-1} from Theorem 4.1. The second-largest singular value σ2​(HX)\sigma_{2}(H_{X}) of HXH_{X} satisfies

σ2​(HX)2=max⁡(λ2​(M0),maxj≠0⁡λmax​(Mj)),\sigma_{2}(H_{X})^{2}\;=\;\max\bigl(\lambda_{2}(M_{0}),\,\max_{j\neq 0}\lambda_{\max}(M_{j})\bigr), (15)

where λ2​(M0)\lambda_{2}(M_{0}) is the second-largest eigenvalue of M0M_{0}. Every non-empty stopping set S⊆VLS\subseteq V_{L} of size aa (Definition 2.4) satisfies

a⁡(m−a​γ2)≤(σ2​(HX)​mγ)2.a\!\left(m-\frac{a\gamma}{2}\right)\;\leq\;\left(\frac{\sigma_{2}(H_{X})\,m}{\gamma}\right)^{\!2}. (16)

Writing C=(σ2​(HX)​m/γ)2C=(\sigma_{2}(H_{X})\,m/\gamma)^{2} and setting a±=(m±m2−2​γ​C)/γa_{\pm}=\bigl(m\pm\sqrt{m^{2}-2\gamma C}\bigr)/\gamma, inequality (16) is informative precisely when σ2​(HX)2<γ/2\sigma_{2}(H_{X})^{2}<\gamma/2; in this regime every non-empty stopping set SS satisfies |S|≤a−|S|\leq a_{-} or |S|≥a+|S|\geq a_{+}, so the stopping distance is bounded below by a+a_{+} whenever the small-size range (0,a−](0,a_{-}] is excluded by separate (e.g. girth- or degree-based) considerations.

Proof.

See Figure 6. By Definition 2.4, a stopping set SS satisfies |N⁡(S)|≤a​γ/2|N(S)|\leq a\gamma/2, since every check in N⁡(S)N(S) has at least two neighbours in SS. For a (γ,k)(\gamma,k)-biregular code with mm checks and nn variables (so |E|=γ​n=k​m|E|=\gamma n=km), the expander mixing lemma applied to the bipartite Tanner graph gives, for any S⊆VLS\subseteq V_{L} and T⊆VRT\subseteq V_{R},

||E⁡(S,T)|−|E|m​n|​S​‖T‖≤σ2​(HX)​|S|​|T|.\bigl|\,|E(S,T)|-\tfrac{|E|}{mn}|S||T|\,\bigr|\;\leq\;\sigma_{2}(H_{X})\sqrt{|S||T|}.

Taking T=VR∖N⁡(S)T=V_{R}\setminus N(S) makes E⁡(S,T)=∅E(S,T)=\emptyset, so the EMI reduces to γ​a​|T|m≤σ2​(HX)​a​|T|\frac{\gamma a|T|}{m}\leq\sigma_{2}(H_{X})\sqrt{a|T|}. Squaring and dividing by a​|T|>0a|T|>0 yields

a​|T|≤(σ2​(HX)​mγ)2.a\,|T|\;\leq\;\left(\frac{\sigma_{2}(H_{X})\,m}{\gamma}\right)^{\!2}.

Substituting |T|=m−|N⁡(S)|≥m−a​γ/2|T|=m-|N(S)|\geq m-a\gamma/2 gives (16). For (15), the DFT block-diagonalisation of Theorem 4.1 identifies spec⁡(HX​HXT)\operatorname{spec}(H_{X}H_{X}^{T}) with the disjoint union of spec⁡(Mj)\operatorname{spec}(M_{j}) over j=0,…,ℓ−1j=0,\ldots,\ell-1. The Perron eigenvalue σ1​(HX)2=γ​k=λmax​(M0)\sigma_{1}(H_{X})^{2}=\gamma k=\lambda_{\max}(M_{0}), and the next-largest eigenvalue in this union is the larger of λ2​(M0)\lambda_{2}(M_{0}) and maxj≠0⁡λmax​(Mj)\max_{j\neq 0}\lambda_{\max}(M_{j}). ∎

Remark 5.2 (Regime of applicability of Proposition 5.1).

The non-vacuity condition σ2​(HX)2<γ/2\sigma_{2}(H_{X})^{2}<\gamma/2 is restrictive. For (γ,k)(\gamma,k)-biregular bipartite graphs the Alon-Boppana-type lower bound [18, 31] forces σ2​(HX)≥γ−1+k−1−o⁡(1)\sigma_{2}(H_{X})\geq\sqrt{\gamma-1}+\sqrt{k-1}-o(1) as ℓ→∞\ell\to\infty, so for the column-weight-33 family of interest (including the [[882,24]][\![882,24]\!] code of Example 3.2, with γ=3\gamma=3, k=6k=6) the inequality is structurally vacuous: σ22≳(2+5)2≈13\sigma_{2}^{2}\gtrsim(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{5})^{2}\approx 13 while γ/2=1.5\gamma/2=1.5. Proposition 5.1 therefore reads as a framework-level statement: it shows how the QC-GHP Fourier matrices control the stopping distance whenever the second singular value can be driven below γ/2\sqrt{\gamma/2}, a regime accessible to designs with substantially larger column weight or to Ramanujan-type lifted-product constructions, rather than to the small-γ\gamma examples of Section 3. Closing this gap, either by a Tanner-style multi-eigenvalue tightening or by replacing the EMI step with a more parameter-aware spectral inequality, remains an open direction.

6 Concluding remarks

We have developed a quantum-specific spectral framework for the lifted-product (QC-GHP) and generalised bicycle Tanner graphs of the leading quantum LDPC constructions. The central tool is the DFT block-diagonalisation of HX​HXTH_{X}H_{X}^{T} (Theorem 4.1), which exploits the two-block tensor form HX=[H~1∣Ir1⊗B~T]H_{X}=[\,\widetilde{H}_{1}\mid I_{r_{1}}\otimes\widetilde{B}^{T}\,] by absorbing the second block into a scalar shift |b⁡(ωj)|2​Ir1|b(\omega^{j})|^{2}I_{r_{1}} and reduces an (r1​ℓ)×(r1​ℓ)(r_{1}\ell)\times(r_{1}\ell) moment-trace computation to ℓ\ell traces of r1×r1r_{1}\times r_{1} Hermitian matrices, extending the classical single-block reductions of Smarandache–Flanagan [43] and Karimi–Banihashemi [27] to the quantum setting. To illustrate applications of the proposed spectral method, we obtain, for generalised bicycle codes, a 44-cycle count through additive energies (Proposition 4.9) and a joint Sidon characterisation of girth 66 echoing Fossorier’s criterion [19] (Corollary 4.11); via the Wang–Dolecek–Wesel triangle bijection [48], a closed-form Fourier count of the (3,3)(3,3) elementary absorbing sets of column-weight-33 QC-GHP codes (Proposition 4.17), addressing a question raised by the framework of Morris, Pllaha, and Kelley [34]; and, through the bipartite expander mixing lemma applied to the second-largest singular value computed from the same Fourier matrices, a spectral-gap lower bound on stopping-set sizes (Proposition 5.1).

We conclude with a few open problems.

  • •

    Higher even-cycle and absorbing-set counts. Extending the closed-form counts beyond 44- and 66-cycles requires the additive 33-energy (T3T_{3}) computations and the girth-88 criterion noted in Remark 4.13, together with a length-2​j2j analogue of the (3,3)(3,3)-to-triangle bijection in order to translate higher cycle counts into absorbing-set counts.

  • •

    Non-vacuous stopping-set bounds. For the column-weight-33 examples studied here the spectral-gap bound is vacuous, since the second singular value exceeds γ/2\sqrt{\gamma/2}. Identifying QC-GHP design parameters, for instance larger column weight or Ramanujan-type lifted-product constructions, under which the bound becomes informative is left for future work, as is a Tanner-style multi-eigenvalue tightening of the expander mixing step.

  • •

    Other elementary absorbing-set types. The (4,2)(4,2) and (4,0)(4,0) absorbing-set cases are accessible in principle through the same spectral data, via induced “K4K_{4} minus an edge” and induced K4K_{4} counts in the variable-node graph, but they require the additional subgraph-elimination corrections sketched in Remark 4.13.
